messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Walter, a 74-year-old tutor, survived Hurricane Delia three years ago when the storm surge flooded the ground-floor tutoring center where he had been working late with a student. He had missed the evacuation order, focused on preparing materials for the next day, and the water rose so quickly that they had to climb onto a high storage shelf. For six hours they listened to debris battering the walls while the chemical stench of fuel and sewage thickened the air. The memory of that smell still arrives without warning—a whiff of something damp on the street, and suddenly his throat tightens and he is back on that shelf, waiting for rescue that might not come. Sometimes, in quieter moments, he can recall the whole scene but feels completely numb, as if he is watching a movie about someone else. That sensation of detachment has become something he reaches for deliberately. Whenever the panic rises, Walter tries to think of the flood as something that happened to a different person, someone he never really knew. Yet he also cannot stop running through that day in his head, fixing on every detail he thinks he should have noticed—the late bulletin he missed, the student's anxious call he dismissed, the tide that seemed unusually high that morning. Ruminating about how the event could have been prevented is the only way he knows to feel even a sliver of control, though it leaves him more exhausted and more convinced that another disaster is waiting.

This sense of looming threat has reshaped his daily life. Walter now scans every room he enters for exits and places where his back is protected. When he tutors, he positions himself against a wall where he can see the whole space, and he refuses to work in rooms without clear sight lines. Even a minor delay—a student arriving ten minutes late, a printer that jams—fills him with the certainty that something terrible is unfolding. The smell of rain on pavement can derail an entire session, sending him into a state of hypervigilance that he cannot hide from his students. His partner has noticed the changes. Walter no longer agrees to impromptu outings or visits to unfamiliar places. He avoids any environment he cannot vet in advance—crowded plazas, restaurants without clear sight lines, any building he has not walked through beforehand. Avoidance of anything that could be stressful has become his primary rule. This has narrowed their life considerably. They eat at the same three restaurants, take the same walking route, and Walter has stopped attending the community events he once enjoyed.

The paradox, which he does not yet see clearly, is that protecting himself from stress has made the world feel more dangerous. The more he avoids, the more his mind generates scenarios of what could go wrong—a blocked exit, a locked door, a sudden crowd pushing him into a corner. And the more he dissociates from the memory, the more forcefully it returns, particularly the smell of damp carpet or diesel exhaust on a warm day, which arrives as a gut punch of recognition that leaves him disoriented for hours. What brought Walter to a therapist was not his own decision. His partner told him gently that she could not keep living this way—that his fear had turned their home into a fortress, and that she missed the man who used to joke with strangers in line at the grocery store. Walter is ashamed of the burden he has placed on her, but what frightens him most is the thought of letting go of these routines. He is certain that if he stops scanning, stops avoiding, stops rehearsing how things could go wrong, the flood will find him again. He wants to believe that therapy can help, but he is terrified that the one thing he has to give up—his constant vigilance—is the only thing keeping him safe.
